MR. MARTIN (ESSEX EAST)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER IN TELEVISION ADDRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Last night the Prime Minister spoke to the nation over the television facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and in the course of that speech he made an announcement of government policy. He referred to the effective date when various amendments to social security measures would be applied in Canada.
I submit to you, sir, that it is within the traditions and practices of parliament that announcements of government policy, while the house is in session, should be made in parliament. I should have thought, Mr. Speaker, that such an announcement by one who in the past has so often regarded himself as one of the champions of parliament would not have been made by that particular right hon. gentleman. I think my question of privilege, sir, is well founded, particularly in view of the fact that on October 22 the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. MARTIN (ESSEX EAST)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER IN TELEVISION ADDRESS
speechtext:
At
page 248.

subtopic: MR. MARTIN (ESSEX EAST)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER IN TELEVISION ADDRESS
speechtext:
-at page 248 of Hansard asked this question of the Minister of National Health and Welfare:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the fact that in the resolutions of which he has given notice calling for amendments to the Old Age Security Act and related statutes he has been good enough to give us all the other details, can he now tell us what is to be the effective date?
The reply of the Minister of National Health and Welfare was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the effective date will appear in the legislation when the bill appears before the house.
Surely last night's statement by the Prime Minister is a violation of the right hon. gentleman's own counsel, and obviously a violation of the rights of parliament.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MR. MARTIN (ESSEX EAST)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER IN TELEVISION ADDRESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say that my hon. friend is apparently hard pressed to find something to which to object-

subtopic: MR. MARTIN (ESSEX EAST)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER IN TELEVISION ADDRESS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MR. MARTIN (ESSEX EAST)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER IN TELEVISION ADDRESS
speechtext: -in order to bring his name before the Canadian public at a time when he is most anxious to have it brought before the public. Any statement I made last evening was a statement which, with the exception of one item, was covered by the resolution. I am one who does not follow a script too closely, and if in a momentary indiscretion I pointed out that it was the intention of the government to have this social security measure begin on November 1, I am sure nobody was harmed.

subtopic: MR. MARTIN (ESSEX EAST)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER IN TELEVISION ADDRESS
speechtext: What about this house you profess to love so much?

subtopic: MR. MARTIN (ESSEX EAST)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER IN TELEVISION ADDRESS
speechtext: Let me say this. If at any time this side of the house or this government commits no more serious indiscretion, if it is such, than happened last night, the people of Canada will continue to be well satisfied with this government; and the opportunity will not be too long delayed to give them that chance to indicate whether or not they were shocked last evening by the revelation which disturbed the hon. gentleman.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR PAYMENT OF COMPENSATION TO APPLE GROWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture, and I do so in a spirit of continuing co-operation with one of his colleagues.
In view of the fact that one of the minister's cabinet colleagues, representing a British Columbia fruit growing district, last year urged the government to compensate the tree fruit growers of British Columbia for their loss of 48 cents per box on the 1955 crop by the granting of a subsidy of not less than 25 cents per box, is the government now giving favourable consideration to the hon. gentleman's representations?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minisier of Agriculture):
maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR PAYMENT OF COMPENSATION TO APPLE GROWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. gentleman for giving me notice of this question. The short answer to it is "no", but I think perhaps I should say a word of general explanation in connection with this matter.
Representations have been received from the British Columbia fruit growers' association and others requesting special grants to compensate British Columbia apple growers for losses alleged to have been suffered by reason of low prices for apples in 1955.
A review of the situation discloses the following facts. The average farm value of apples in British Columbia in 1954 was $1.24

per bushel. In 1955 the corresponding figure was 72 cents. In 1956 the farm value Tose to $1.34 per bushel, the highest in the past 10 years. These figures are all substantially higher than the average farm value of apples for all Canada in the corresponding years.
In the light of these facts and the relative position of British Columbia apple growers compared with those in other parts of Canada, it does not seem possible or practicable to offer any special compensation to British Columbia growers.

They were not afraid of starting a precedent when they sold wheat under the British wheat agreement, under which the farmers lost about $431 million. They were not afraid of a precedent when they sold wheat at the same time for the same price, which was less than the world market price, to the Canadian millers and the Canadian consumers, and the farmers lost an additional $136 million. They were not afraid of a precedent when they took about $500 million out of the farmers' pockets, out of my pocket and out of my neighbour's pocket and out of everybody else's pockets on the farms in western Canada who were selling grain at that time. They were not afraid of a precedent when they passed the Prairie Grain Producers' Interim Financing Act to protect the banks and see that the bankers got their 5 per cent interest. But when we get a little bill on the floor of this house, such as we have here today, they become worried and say it is a dangerous precedent.
I feel that perhaps we should have started a precedent of this kind a long time ago, a precedent to give the farmers a break for a change, and give them what is rightfully theirs instead of continually taking it away from them. There have been strong hints by some that this bill is subsidizing the agricultural industry and western farmers. There have also been strong hints that the agricultural industry must compete in world markets. So far as I have been able to follow them, these hints are coming mostly from members who have no agricultural industry, or very little, in their ridings.
Let me say to these hon. gentlemen that the agricultural industry has been subsidizing other industries through tariffs and other regulations almost ever since those other industries started. What is more, rumours are abroad that they want more protection and more subsidies from the farm people, who will eventually pay them. Rumours are that some of these other industries want increases in tariffs on steel. They also want increased tariffs on half a dozen other items.
[Mr. Stefura.l
They want it today when the farmer is caught in a price squeeze. Farm prices have dropped to such an extent that farm people, in many instances, have a hard time trying to hang on. On the other hand, the prices of everything the farmer has to buy have gone up, and they find it difficult to hang on in the other way.
Some people call it price squeeze. I call it a tug of war. They are pulling the farmer apart. Under these conditions we have some of our Liberal members defending the interim financing act. I say that policy is not in the best interests of the farm people. All it does is put an additional burden on the farm people, and it is just pulling them apart in three directions. The farmer must go to the bank and borrow at 5 per cent interest. Therefore I say the interim financing act was certainly some plan for western agriculture.
To those who say that the farmers should compete in world markets under present conditions, I say remove your tariffs for the farm people and the agricultural industry and then you may have a good argument. But under present conditions, when the farm people are contributing to the prices of many of these industries the argument does not hold. If you feel that the farm people must compete in world markets, then give the farmer the privilege of buying on the world market without those tariffs and customs duties and all the legal red tape. Let the farmer sell his products for gold or sterling, or barter for goods with any country that suits him. Give the farm people a free hand to do business in the way they see fit, and in a way that they have been asking to do business for years through their farm organizations and through whatever means they have at their disposal. I am sure there would then be no need for any emergency measures such as we have before us in the house today.
I trust the present government realizes that this is only an emergency measure and that legislation must be brought in to get at the root of the ills that we have in the agricultural industry today. I trust that this government will not use this bill as a cure-all for these ills, because the agricultural industry is going to require a lot of legislation to give it a parity of income.
I am confident that this bill having to do with cash advances, as proposed, will not do the job to the extent that the present Minister of Finance believes it will. It allows only 50 cents a bushel for wheat stored on the farm; it allows only a 6-bushel quota. The farmers will be able to get about $600, $800 or perhaps $900. That, I submit, is a long way from the actual need

Grain
or requirement, when we consider that the farmer must pay taxes; he must pay his store bills, fuel bills ond so on. The $600 or $800 will not go very far. This government must give immediate and careful consideration to increasing storage space and to the idea of a food bank; it must give careful consideration to promoting sales by such means as accepting sterling, barter or extending credit to countries which may be short of hard currency at this time.
I asked the Minister of Finance a question on October 23 as follows, as recorded at page 313 of Hansard:
Has the government given consideration to the acceptance of sterling in an effort to increase Canadian exports to Britain and other commonwealth nations? If so, has a decision been reached, and what was the nature of that decision?
I was very much surprised to receive the following answer:
No such proposal was made to the Canadian government.
I repeated the question on page 314 of Hansard and received the following answer:
I have already told my hon. friend that question has not even been raised by anyone.
We had about 12 joint meetings that were sponsored by the Alberta farmers union in our constituency, and all the candidates were present. When the question would come up as to how the Conservatives planned to increase foreign trade, the acceptance of sterling was at the top of the list. The Conservative candidate is a fine old gentleman. I have nothing at all against him personally. I do not for a moment want to believe, nor can I find that I can do so, that he would manufacture his own policy. If the minister denies that it was a campaign promise made by Conservative candidates, then perhaps he can explain why the candidates take a Social Credit policy, a policy which the Social Crediters have been presenting to this house for years and then wish to get elected as Conservative members of this house. To present policies and hope to get elected on policies that the ministers have never even heard presented to them as questions is definitely misleading the people. We can never hope to have good government or to give the people the kind of administration they so desire if we deliberately mislead those people in our country.
I urge the members of this house to get this bill through as a temporary measure to aid agriculture and give the government a chance to introduce legislation which will cure the basic ills of agriculture. The policies that brought agriculture to its present condition have been in effect for a long time, and it cannot be expected that they can be cured over night. However, the sooner you 96698-33
get down to the basic problems, the sooner you will be able to restore the agricultural industry to its rightful place in our economy. (Translation):

Mr. Speaker, in speaking on this bill which is to provide advance payments to farmers who cannot sell their grain, I find myself in a rather awkward position. 1 do not like the measure in its present form, but I cannot possibly oppose it because I am one of those who have been advocating emergency assistance for years. I am thankful the government has acceded to the request, and I will support the measure. No matter how little benefit the farmers will receive from it, I will support it on the assumption that in this case something is better than nothing.
However, I feel I would be remiss in my duty if I were not to point out the shortcomings of this legislation. I only hope I can find the right words to do that and not be misunderstood, especially at a time when there is such an acute mortality prevailing amongst the members of this parliament. I am not against the principle of this measure, but I must indicate the inadequacies compared with the needs. Perhaps I should not do this, because everyone seems to be fairly well satisfied with the bill. I know the farmers are badly in need of this support.
In mentioning the weaknesses of this bill before us I find myself about in the same position as a lay observer watching a doctor perform an emergency operation on a dying person. He would think twice, at least, before he would tap the doctor's shoulder and offer advice in the moment when the doctor was performing that vital and delicate incision. I think he would rather be inclined to keep his mouth shut, for such an interruption might irritate the doctor and cause his hand to shake, thus endangering a life. I would not want to do that at this point. I shall therefore try to be careful in choosing my words to express my disappointment at the value of this government action.
Perhaps I can do this best by using the well known phrase coined during wartime; "too little and too late". In order to make a proper analysis I would divide the phrase into two parts. I would concentrate on the "late" part first by saying that what we are 06698-33i
Grain
doing now should have been done years ago, and should have been done in much fuller measure than we are attempting to do now. The former government was confronted with this request year after year, but they refused to even consider it. It was branded a wild idea, an unreasonable demand, absolutely impossible to implement. Now that we have a new government the farmers' petition is granted in principle at least, and the former minister of agriculture wants to get in on the credit. He tried hard the other day to make out a case for himself, and in his desperation he went so far as to intimate that this step could have been taken before if it had not been for the backward farm organizations. They did not even ask for it.
At this point I should like to make it clear that if the right hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner) wants to use the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to shield himself from an embarrassing position it is quite all right with me. Perhaps he is even justified in doing so. This organization has provided a barricade behind which he and the former minister of trade and commerce have hidden for years, and perhaps that is one of the reasons we have not got advance payments yet.
However, when the right hon. member goes so far as to indicate that all farm organizations have been against the idea of cash advances, then he should know he cannot get away with such backstage manoeuvring in this parliament. I have with me the last three briefs presented by the interprovincial farm union council to the government. The first one was presented on February 16, 1956, and on page 15 it says:
Therefore, the interprovincial farm union councils continuing to press for adoption of its original proposal (which has been endorsed at the three wheat pool delegate meetings) that the government arrange for interest-free cash advances by the Canadian wheat board on farm-stored grain to the value of 50 per cent of the initial payment on an estimated delivery of 8 bushels per cultivated acre.
This proves that the proposal was made and that it had been adopted by three wheat pool meetings. The next brief was presented on February 19, 1957. On page 8, it asks that a permanent system of cash advances be established on the basis recommended in previous submissions in order that farmers will have the means to meet their annual obligations. This should be enough to destroy the validity of the assertion made by the former minister of trade and commerce which was seized upon by

Grain
the hon. member for Melville. The next brief was presented on August 15, 1957 in which the same request is repeated.
This I am sure will do away with any implications that our farm organizations were against advance payments. Where did the idea come from in the first place if it was not from the farm organizations? if the Liberal government had been as interested in the farmers as were some of the farm organizations then the farmers would not today be in a position of having to ask for emergency assistance.
The government could have prevented the situation by adopting a more aggressive attitude in selling our wheat; other people are selling their wheat. The United States exported 535 million bushels last year while Canada exported only 260 million bushels. Is there one natural reason why the United States should be able to sell one single bushel more than Canada, when our wheat has been recognized as the best in the world? Our wheat is hard wheat which some countries are forced to buy whereas the United States wheat is soft wheat which can be obtained anywhere.
Our final certificate covering export sales is accepted with the same confidence as a certified cheque. In contrast, the United States grading system, from No. 1 to the lowest, is inferior to ours in every respect. Nevertheless they almost doubled their sales last year when they exported 275 million bushels more than we did. In the same period our sales went down 49 million bushels. What is the reason for this difference? Could it be that those who were in charge of the development of policies for the United States wheat disposal program had enough imagination to conceive of strategies and approaches which have proved successful while those who were responsible for our program lacked incentive and vision to the point where they are relying on an orthodox trade policy and waiting for Santa Claus to bring them some customers?
United States policy makers have used four different ways in which to introduce a progressive sales policy: sales for American dollars, sales for local currency, barter trade and other relief assistance. Instead of adopting at least some of these various beneficial methods our government embarked on a course of criticism which to my mind is senseless to the highest degree, degrading those who do it, stifling business and resulting in a danger to this country.
When my neighbours sell faster and better than I do, do I criticize them? Of course not. I will find out how they do it and learn something.

In the 1955-56 crop year the United States exported 344 million bushels of wheat of which 97 million were sold for dollars, 93 million bushels for foreign currency, 67 million bushels were barter transactions, and 87 million bushels were exchanged under a mutual aid and relief program. If our government had adopted similar progressive sales policies during the years we would not have to find the cost of storage which now amounts to about $100 million a year and which includes some farm storage costs, but we could have sold a large portion of our wheat when the price was high. How much the farmers have lost in this respect alone can be seen from the fact that at the opening of the crop year 1953 the price of No. 1 Northern wheat was $2.03 a bushel and on July 21, 1957 the price was $1.61, a loss of 42 cents in four years. In last year alone wheat prices dropped by 12 cents a bushel.
Farmers have not only lost in sales and prices at the export level but also at the domestic level. From 1947 to 1953 the export price ranged from $2.00 to $3.40 a bushel but our domestic price was held down by the government and ranged from $1.55 to $2.55. When you know of these facts it is rather amusing to listen to those hon. members on the Liberal side who have voted against the resolution talk about discrimination and to those who with tears in their eyes talk about the United States give-away program and the terrible sums of money it costs the people of the United States. You never hear anybody talk about the Canadian giveaway program for which these farmers alone had to pay; no one mentions the United Kingdom wheat agreement which cost the western farmers in the neighbourhood of a $300 to $400 million; no one talks about the millions and millions of dollars paid by the farmers in storage charges.
This is the way western farmers have been backed up against the wall to the point where they are now forced to ask for emergency assistance. I am happy this government seems to recognize that fact, at least to some extent, and has brought down a measure which is a step in the right direction, but it is still too late and too little. In dealing with the too little aspect I want to say that in speaking in the debate in reply to the speech from the throne the other day I made it clear that no half measures are good enough at this time.
Unfortunately this first legislation brought down by this government will no doubt be exactly that. Six bushels an acre is only half of the normal crop; what about the other half? Can farmers at this time afford to get only half their payment on merely half their crop? What about last year's crop?

What about the crop from the year before? It is most unfortunate that in this case this government is doing to the farmer something similar to what the former government did to our senior citizens. The advance payment on only 6 bushels an acre compares, I suggest, with the measly $6 increase in pensions which was granted last session. Will the farmers be more satisfied with this treatment than the old age pensioners were?
What is the material difference between this bill and the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act, aside from the interest, which in this case is paid by the government, and the fact that it is received by the farmer as a matter of right. Apart from that there is no difference. A farmer cannot obtain any more money under this act than he could under last year's act. As a matter of fact, he would get less. Under the provisions of the interim finance act a producer could borrow up to $3,000 if he had the grain to cover that sum, but under this proposal the amount of grain a farmer has in store does not matter; it is acreage which counts, not grain. A farmer has to have 1,000 acres before he can get $3,000. Furthermore, he can only get this amount if he grows only wheat. If he grows barley or oats he will get less. Is this the best this government can do?
Let us take, for example, an average farmer with a half section of land and 270 specified acres. If his production is all in wheat, he will receive $810; if in barley, $567; and if in oats, $324. This shows clearly how little benefit those hard-pressed farmers who have reached the end of their rope in financing their operations can hope to get out of this legislation if no changes are made.
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Proven-cher (Mr. Jorgenson), speaking on the resolution last week, expressed the opinion that farmers are a reasonable group of people and that they will, therefore, be satisfied with this proposal. I have reached the opposite view. It will be the reasonable people who will recognize the fact that this is a feeble effort on the part of the government. They will see that this gesture is not only of little assistance to the average farmer but will create an incentive to grow more wheat, which is most dangerous. By allowing advances only on six bushels an acre regardless of the grain delivered, and then graduating the amount he receives from fifty cents for wheat to thirty-five for barley and twenty cents for oats, he may be inclined to grow the grain that brings the most money under this arrangement as it stands.
Mr. Speaker, it is hard to understand how hon. members of this house can stand up, speak on this bill and assert that everything
Grain
is really quite all right, when some of its features are so obviously all wrong. There is plenty of evidence that this legislation in its present form is not only inadequate but is disturbing in some respects. For example, I point out sub-clause 4 of clause 3, which reads as follows:
No person who has received an advance payment under this act in any crop year is, until his undertaking in respect thereof has been fully discharged, entitled to receive an advance payment in any subsequent crop year.
This means, in simple terms, that if a farmer is unable to deliver his six bushels allowed under the quota by the end of the crop year he cannot get any advance on his new crop until he delivers his old quota and discharges his obligations.

Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) or the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), who has taken his place today can guarantee us that we can deliver six bushels this year I shall be not only satisfied but gratified by his assurance. But only a very cheerful optimist would dare to make such a prediction at this stage in the present circumstances. We could not do it last year, at least in my constituency, and I do not think it can be done this year either.
There is only one way in which it could be done: we must sell more grain than we are doing now. So far there is no evidence of such a trend. All signs point to the fact that up to now no all-out effort has been made to cope with this problem in a practical manner and, therefore, our present position can be described without fear of contradiction as a pitiful and deplorable stalemate. We are forced to accept it as such until the minister sees his way clear to tell this house what his plans are. We know that he is confronted with one of the most complicated problems, and we appreciate his position. We do not expect that he should sell all this wheat overnight, but I do feel that he and those who work with him should by now have been able to figure out some idea, some plan or some action that may be taken. So far he has said nothing that satisfies my curiosity or which does justice to the urgency of the situation.
From the minister's silence in this house and the address he made in Winnipeg to the national dairy council of Canada I have

Grain
reached the conclusion that those who are in charge of our present grain marketing problem are tarred with the same brush of fear that has caused the indecision which has plagued that group for years. They seem to be, in a sense, prisoners of the past who have failed to respond to the challenges of the present.
Commenting on the minister's speech in Winnipeg, the Western Producer has this to say:
After making due allowance for the handicaps under which he suffered it must, we fear, be admitted that Mr. Churchill was disappointing. His speech sounded dull and pedestrian, contained little that was new or inspiring and indeed would not have sounded much out of place coming from the mouth of a spokesman for the former regime.
How true this analysis is was proven by the minister when in the same speech he fell into the old rut of criticizing those who do something to dispose of their surpluses, and blaming them in the main for the reduction of our sales.
It is a sorry picture, when farmers are economically bankrupt while sitting on a pile of wheat to the magnitude of one billion bushels, to see those who are responsible for our sales program doing little more than criticize those who do something. Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has joined from time to time the parade of critics.
Perhaps it is true that we should not follow exactly in the footsteps of the United States in disposing of our surplus, but we should, indeed we must, find means to distribute our surplus wheat to those who need it even if they cannot pay for it in dollars. Every fair-minded observer must admit that our present method of selling for dollars only has failed us miserably. At the same time the United States, by her easy selling terms, has disposed of considerable quantities of wheat to needy people who have not the money to pay in the ordinary way.
Unfortunately, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) made it clear the other day that this government has no intention of taking the initiative in investigating the possibility of selling wheat for sterling or other local currency. On October 23, 1957, as reported at page 315 of Hansard of that date, the Minister of Finance made this statement:
-until some of the countries on a sterling basis regard this as a matter of sufficient importance to them to come and ask us to accept such an arrangement, I do not see any reason why we should go out proposing to take sterling.
We are still acting in an independent manner as if we were in a seller's market. It is difficult to follow this line of reasoning. The minister made this comment in spite of the fact that from November 15, 1954, to April 30, 1957, the United States has signed 92 agreements with 32 countries to the value of

$1.8 billion which covered 446 million bushels of wheat. Twenty-three of these countries received wheat in exchange for local currencies. For some reason our authorities seem to be afraid to tackle this problem in a progressive manner. They have taken the passive course which has always proven to be most unsafe in the competitive business world. Those in charge do not seem to realize that this situation demands a high order of creativeness and instead of being afraid of doing something they should be afraid of doing nothing. If they would move we would not need to waste our time today talking about providing emergency assistance nor would we have had to waste millions upon millions of dollars in storage charges. We have paid enough unnecessary storage charges in the past few years to pay for at least half of that surplus wheat and give it away.
Our new Minister of Trade and Commerce made it clear in his speech that he has no intention of changing the policy of storing surplus wheat. On August 30,	1957, as
reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of that date, he is reported as having said in that city:
I hold the view that our higher grades of wheat might better be kept in store rather than given away or sold at cut rate prices.
And so we are sitting on our pile of surplus wheat and apparently the government intends to let the farmer and the nation pay storage until they are blue in the face. We will continue to sit on it even though it has become a crushing burden to western farmers and in spite of the fact that over half of the world's population is going to bed hungry every night. That we cannot dispose of our surpluses in a hungry world is a disgrace to our intelligence and those who brought us to this point should hang their heads in shame.
They are responsible for the creation of the situation in which we now find ourselves of being forced to pass emergency legislation to alleviate this deplorable condition. Measures designed and saturated with the same platitudes which are partly responsible for the plight of the western farmer will not come near the mark in terms of solving this problem. Apparently the government is still hoping that some day, somehow this problem will solve itself by some semimiraculous means involving no effort on its part. It is hoping against hope that the problem will vanish of its own accord.

Mr. Speaker, I had not planned to take part in the discussion on this bill which, I contend, is

one of extreme urgency for a certain part of our population. However, I would not like either, by keeping silent, to give the population of this country the impression that members on the government side are opposed to an emergency measure designed to give western farmers some money until this year's crop is sold.
It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker-this is my maiden speech in this house but I am being forced by circumstances, to take part in this debate-that I feel it my duty, indeed a sacred duty, as a representative of an essentially agricultural constituency of the province of Quebec, to speak in the French language, the language of my electors.
Mr. Speaker, I know for having discussed this matter in caucus and in discussions with the Prime Minister that this is an urgent measure. This is no grant, no outright gift made by the country to western farmers but, for all practical purposes, a loan which will provide them with ready cash until such time as their crop is sold. That is why I would like to take a clear stand on this issue, as did other Quebec members who spoke before me.
I would not like this measure offered by the government to be considered as a gift. I know that this legislation does not apply to the other farm products, but I know also that it is a part of the policy announced by the Prime Minister in order to achieve balance in the field of agriculture. I support it, though, because I have as much feeling as those members who preceded me.
This plan is not perfect because perfection is not of this world but we shall try to reduce the margin existing at this time between prices obtained by the producers and what the consumers pay. Being a farmer's son and the owner of a farm, I know that the price obtained by the farmer for his products does not provide him with a salary comparable to that of other classes of society at the present time.
That is why we will shortly propose legislation with a view to filling this gap between the price paid to the producer and the price paid by the consumer.
Therein lies, I think, the difficulty facing the farmers of the province of Quebec. I had intended to deal with various aspects of agriculture in the province of Quebec during the debate on the address in reply to the
Grain
speech from the throne, but the examination of this measure prompted me to say a few words on the question of loans or grants to western farmers.

If they remember well, in March and April 1956 maple syrup was selling at $7 a gallon in my riding. This year, the same syrup, of identical quality, sold at $3 a gallon. And yet, it was not the Conservative party which was in power. Therefore, it is not our fault, it is a legacy for which we cannot be held accountable, but, nonetheless a legacy that we have come into. This bill, this loan we are suggesting is, in other words, an advance on their crops, which is going to be refunded to the federal treasury through their wheat pools. It is not an amount of $2.5 million which they are going to keep, but a cash advance.

that should be restated and kept in mind in considering the agricultural measure now before us.
The position of this group relative to the matter under consideration has been declared very clearly and concisely not only in the course of this debate but on other occasions as well. Recognizing as we do the serious financial difficulty in which the wheat producers of the prairie provinces find themselves owing to the inability to market their grain we have supported and do support the principle of cash advances on farm-stored grain as proposed in the measure. However, once again I would like to call attention to what I consider to be a very serious weakness or, shall I say, a danger in the legislation which we are now considering.
We are singling out a particular section of our country and a specific part of our agricultural industry for special attention. Let me again state, as I have already done, this proposal is receiving my support, but I do feel that in this parliament we must concern ourselves with policies and measures the benefits of which will, in comparable circumstances, be available to citizens right across our country. As an illustration, I should like to refer just briefly to our plea made on other occasions for the expansion of such measures as the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I mention this at this time only to illustrate my point.
Our agricultural industry, or economy, in British Columbia is, as you know Mr. Speaker, more diversified but we have marketing problems as well. We feel that as regards at least some of our products we might be justified in claiming some such assistance as is contemplated in this measure. I am reminded as well of the maritime section, and the producers in that area who might feel justified in requesting consideration, and no doubt would benefit considerably were the benefits of such legislation made available to them.
Some months ago I had the opportunity to be in the province of New Brunswick and the problem of marketing their potato crop was brought to my attention. When the crop is harvested the markets are usually in a very depressed condition; but because of the desperate position in which the producers find themselves they dispose of their potato crop to buyers or speculators at a few cents a barrel. Those potatoes are stored on the farms by those producers and when the markets improve and a good price is commanded the buyers come along and take delivery and, of course, reap the benefits. I would suggest that if some such legislation was passed, or if a provision was included 
in such a measure as we have here, cash advances in that particular instance would be of inestimable value to the producers of that section. If those advances were available they could store their crop just as they do at the present time but they themselves would benefit from the improved market at the time of selling. I know it would be very hard on the speculators but it would be good for the producers.
I raise this point, Mr. Speaker, not because of any opposition to the principle involved in this measure but because I and many others are of the opinion that the benefits of measures designed for the good of our people should be available to all under comparable circumstances.
I listened with a great deal of interest to some of the members who participated in the debate last evening, for instance the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith). I was charmed by his quality of voice; I enjoyed his powers of oratory but I could not appreciate, as can be understood, his wholehearted confidence in the present administration to carry through a program that in its totality would take care of all the problems that face agriculture at the present time. I believe one of the other members suggested that this was only the first in a list of measures which would be introduced by this government and which would be in the interests of the agricultural industry of the nation. My own fear, Mr. Speaker, is that unless the fires are kept burning and a good head of steam is maintained this government may grind to a stop before the destination is reached, before the point is reached where legislation has been brought in which will bring to the agricultural industry of Canada the help it needs at the present time. Therefore, I raise this point once again, Mr. Speaker, in the hope that when measures are introduced in this house we shall keep in mind the fact that we are dealing with national issues, and the measures which are contemplated, considered and passed should be in the interest of all the people of Canada regardless of where they may reside. Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to take this opportunity to say a few words on this bill which provides for cash advances. It is not my purpose to oppose the measure. I think the measure is long overdue. The people of Canada, and particularly the farmers of western Canada, have been forced into a position where they are nearly bankrupt. It does not make any difference what government is in power; the result would be the same. Because of the great demands being made and the situation of the western farmer, any government which was in power would be obliged to put this legislation through.
We well recall that when the Conservatives, who now form the government, were in opposition they, along with the Social Crediters and C.C.F., on every occasion protested the dire situation in which farmers found themselves. We all pressed for some assistance in the form of cash advances to the farmers of western Canada. The fact that the present government is introducing this measure does not alter the fact that it would have been introduced by any party which formed the government.
I think it can be truly said, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of western Canada have found themselves in very poor financial circumstances. Because of a lack of a sales policy by the former government, and certainly because of the lack of a sales policy by the present government, this measure is a necessity. The farmers, not only in my constituency but in nearly all western constituencies, have found themselves in a position where they were forced to sell grain at cut-rate prices to any source that was available in order to secure cash to carry on from day to day. The farmers in my constituency, and in other constituencies, were forced to sell their grain at 50 cents to 60 cents a bushel. All hon. members who

were in the opposition protested strenuously to the government and requested the inauguration of a system of cash advances so that farmers would not be forced by their creditors to sell grain at cut-rate prices and thereby lose hundreds of thousands of dollars.
I want to say a word, Mr. Speaker, about the attitude taken the other day by one of the members, the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). I can appreciate his situation and his statement that under this measure no assistance is being given to the Atlantic provinces. I would suggest to him, however, that rather than take the attitude that he would vote against this measure he should support the measure and then make every effort to have this government and this house introduce legislation to give the people of the maritimes some relief. Conservative governments have been in power for some time in the maritimes, in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and they have done little, if anything, for those two provinces. After all, surely the position has been established that in modern society those who toil, those who do this nation's work, should be entitled to holidays, not just when there is illness, not just when there is unemployment, but as a matter of right, and with sufficient pay to enable them to enjoy those holidays.
As hon. members are aware, this principle has been accepted to a considerable extent by the provinces. Six provinces have general

Industrial Relations
legislation in this field-British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec. In addition to those six, a seventh, namely New Brunswick, has enacted legislation covering some of its workers. The legislation in these provinces varies as to the extent of the holidays guaranteed; it varies also as to the point at which holidays come into effect, but there are at least two provinces whose legislation provides what this bill seeks, namely two weeks' holidays after one year's service. Those two provinces which are at the top of the list are the provinces of British Columbia and Saskatchewan.
It is our view in presenting this bill, and it was the view held in the last parliament by those who spoke to this legislation on the Conservative side of the house, that this is the kind of matter with regard to which the federal government should give a lead. We recognize that so far as labour questions are concerned we have a divided jurisdiction in this country; the greater portion of our industrial workers comes under provincial labour jurisdiction, leaving only some 9 or 10 per cent under federal labour jurisdiction.
It is to that group that this bill would specifically apply, but we feel that there would be more to it, when enacted, than simply its direct benefits. In addition to providing the type of benefit it does for this group of people, if the federal parliament would enact legislation of this kind it would give a lead to the provinces and hasten the day when it will be a universally accepted fact, recognized in law, that workers are fully entitled to the benefit of holidays with pay, and that it should be not less than the period set out in this bill, namely, two weeks after one year's service.
Mr. Speaker, as members of this house know-at least those who have sat in this house before-the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is quite capable of occupying the full 40 minutes allowed to a member, but I do not think it is necessary to do so in connection with this bill. The matter has been debated several times in the house before, and it is something to which all parties are committed. I therefore hope that now that the measure is before the house it will receive support from the same quarters which supported it previously, namely my own party, the Conservative party and the Social Credit party. I hope too, that the Liberals will also see the light and go along with this bill so that it may become law.
I join with the Canadian Labour Congress in welcoming the fact that the new government has seen fit to propose legislation of this kind. As hon. members may know, it just so happened that having introduced this bill on previous occasions I caused it to be introduced

on the very first day of this new session so that it is on the order paper ahead of the government's bill. I think that is a fortunate circumstance, for it means that the house can now come to grips, not only with the issue of holidays with pay but also with the issue of the length of holiday after one year's service that should now be the case. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have much pleasure in presenting this bill and I hope that the evidence I have given will indicate that it should now be passed by this House of Commons.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ANNUAL VACATIONS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this occasion with some diffidence but I would like to say a few words in respect to the bill which is being proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). As has already been clearly intimated it is the intention of the government to introduce legislation which, it seems clear, from what has been said, respects the same principles that apparently are the concern of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Annual paid vacations for workers are now generally recognized as desirable for the health, welfare and efficiency of employees. The major principle of any legislation directed to a subject matter of this sort is to ensure that a minimum period of paid vacations should be provided in law as one of the conditions of employment which an employer must be prepared to make effective in application to his employees.

In my opinion provisions for annual paid vacations for workers should not be left wholly in the discretion of employers or left entirely to collective bargaining. I feel that there should be federal vacations with pay legislation to complement the legislation enacted by the great majority of provinces in this field. Annual vacation plans more favourable than the minimum standard which the government legislation may contain in my opinion may be properly left to collective bargaining or to individual arrangements. I recognize that it is only by means of legislation that there can be an assurance that all workers whether organized or unorganized, and the welfare of everyone of whom must be our very real concern, will have an annual vacation with pay and that it will conform to a reasonable minimum standard.
It now remains to decide what constitutes a reasonable minimum standard in so far as legislation making provision for it is concerned. We have to bear in mind that vacations represent a cost to the employer and in my view a balance must be struck between the cost it is reasonable to impose on the employer by legislation, on the one hand, and the standards it is reasonable to require for workers, on the other. The effect on collective bargaining is a consideration that cannot escape us either.
The employer who makes an improvement in his vacation policy through collective bargaining or as required by legislation or otherwise will probably feel that this lessens his ability to grant wage increases or reduces the size of the wage increase he can afford to grant. On the other hand it may be assumed that a worker who enjoys an adequate annual vacation is a more productive worker. Thus it is very difficult to measure in cents per hour the exact cost to an employer of providing a vacation for his workers. These are matters that are threshed out around a bargaining table.
A union and an employer may decide to make improvements in vacation practices, in wages or in the pension plan but it will be mutually recognized that the employer may not be able to afford to do everything the union wants and they may both agree that improvements in the pension plan, for example, are more desirable than improvements in respect to the provisions of the plan in so far as vacations are concerned.
The essential point I think we should all bear in mind in considering legislation of this kind is that the legislative standard for vacations be not so high as to intrude unnecessarily upon the processes of collective bargaining but that it be high enough to establish a reasonable and adequate
Industrial Relations
annual holiday standard and provide assurance of protection to those employees who are in need of it.
In considering what constitutes a proper standard it strikes me that we have to look at the practice prevailing in Canadian industry including those industries which come within federal jurisdiction and we must also look at the legislative provisions adopted by the provinces. Some type of plan with an annual vacation of at least one week's duration is almost universal in Canadian industry. Vacations of two and three weeks are also common and, here and there, even four-week vacations are making an appearance. The practice most commonly found in Canadian industry is to relate the length of the vacation to the length of service of the employee; thus plant workers in manufacturing customarily receive one week's vacation after their first year of employment, a two-week vacation after three to five years' service, and a three-week vacation after service of 15 years. There are variations in vacation policy but our research would indicate that these are the most widely adopted practices. Office workers on the other hand usually get two weeks' vacation after their first year of employment. These practices, an investigation indicates, are widely found in Canadian industry generally and they are also common in industries which fall within the federal jurisdiction.
I would like to say a word or two in reference to the standards set by legislation in effect in some of the provinces. The provinces of Ontario and Quebec set a minimum standard of one week with pay for each year of service. This, as I understand it, is also the standard adopted in New Brunswick in the case of the mining and construction industries. In the case of Alberta and Manitoba, they require one week after one year of employment and two weeks each year after a longer period of service, two years in Alberta and three years in Manitoba. Saskatchewan and British Columbia require two weeks after one year of employment.
Now in the light of the study we have given to this subject we would not agree that any legislation to be proposed to this house in respect to vacation practice should provide merely for a one-week vacation. On the other hand, three-week vacations are not legislated for in any jurisdiction and they hardly constitute a minimum standard.
It strikes me that we have to address ourselves to what constitutes a reasonable service requirement. To provide two weeks after only one year would not in my opinion be a reasonable minimum legislative standard since it is not commonly found in existing

Industrial Relations
provincial legislation, nor in practice, other than in the case, as I have already mentioned, of office workers. To provide two weeks after two years service is somewhat ahead of prevailing practice for non-office workers, and it is a little ahead of the legislative standards provided in a majority of the provinces.
In the light of all the factors I have mentioned it strikes me that what appears to be embodied in the bill which will be presented later on by the government, if it should be afforded the opportunity, and the standard contemplated in its proposed legislation make it the sounder of the two plans that this house will have an opportunity to consider.
The impact of legislation of this kind on industries within federal jurisdiction will be appreciable, even if it is not in the precise form proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. About 5,000 such workers are now employed in establishments which do not now grant two-week vacations. In most of the remaining establishments the effect will be confined to new employees who will now receive benefits which they otherwise would not enjoy.
Under the legislation the government has in mind the employees will certainly be assured-and many of them are not at present-of receiving to a very satisfactory degree the same benefits and privileges that are envisaged or contemplated in the bill of the hon. member now before the house for consideration.
It is in the light of the remarks I have just made that I would ask the hon. members to consider the legislation that is now before us.

I had made some preparation this afternoon to discuss the measure having to do with holidays with pay and had not expected that this bill would come before the house. However, there should be no difficulty in one making up one's mind as to the necessity for assuring every worker in this country at last a minimum of two weeks holiday with pay.
Legislation of this kind was introduced many years ago in the province of British Columbia by a former Liberal premier. Every workman has a holiday book and he, in one way or another, after working one month is provided with stamps which he inserts and which show that he has worked a month. I understand it transpires that after working 12 months he is entitled to two weeks

holiday with pay. But, of course, the debate now resolves itself into whether we should support the measure brought forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) or the measure which is being introduced by the government.
The government had enough confidence in the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to offer him a very responsible position in this house. I wonder whether they should not just accept the legislation brought forward by the hon. member. It differs so little, the exception being that it assures everyone of two weeks pay.
The matter of procedure and order was raised and subsequently dealt with by the Speaker, which does leave me with some apprehension as to what might be the result if this measure introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre were defeated. If, as Mr. Speaker has indicated, a decision has been rendered and it should be an adverse one, then it follows that the bill could not be re-introduced. Whether the government bill has proceeded far enough so that it is not a question of it being re-introduced is perhaps a matter for decision, but before the vote is taken certainly the house should be made aware of the procedure that may be followed.
It is true that in industry and no doubt in government service there is some difference with respect to the length of service and as to the number of days or weeks holiday that one may expect to receive, but certainly a one-week holiday is not a holiday. In these days of enlightenment, when very often in industry we have a four-day weekend,-that is only considered a long weekend-five days is a normal work week in Canada. Hence one week cannot be considered as a holiday. Two weeks should be the minimum that anyone would be receiving.
In the particular industry in which I work, after a year's service the employee receives a two weeks' holiday with pay; after 15 years service he receives a three weeks' holiday with pay; and after having attained the 25-year mark, he is eligible for a four weeks' holiday with pay. Of course, he has been normally working a five-day week. That is something which we do not expect to be put into legislation but we should not be niggardly and expect anyone to have less than the actual two weeks.
There is another aspect of this matter. It has been reported that this winter unemployment may reach the 900,000 mark or even the 1 million mark. We have found, particularly in our industry, that the giving of holidays requires quite a large amount of extra labour. Some of it may be temporary labour, but in

the main it requires a larger staff. In the face of this impending disaster, if it comes about -and certainly the situation is serious enough at this present moment-I think that the government should either incorporate in their legislation this bill which has been introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre or decide to move an amendment of their own which will give the same coverage. I do not remember whether or not I was here at the moment when the vote was taken.

Mr. Speaker, if this legislation means anything at all I think it should be that it is intended to give immediate relief to the farmers who are in dire need of cash. It is, I believe, well understood or it should be, by every member of this house that the only possible way the farmer has been able to keep going at all is by the local grocery man, the local butcher and machine agent supplying the farmers with goods, repairs and machinery on time; in other words, they have been financing these farmers.
It was hoped that this legislation would provide a means whereby the farmers would get a little cash to meet these obligations, because it goes without saying that these people who have been assisting the farmers cannot long continue to finance them. Therefore the cash which is to be given through

cash advances should be intended tor use in relieving these local financial obligations, but according to clause 18 of the bill something of a damper is put on that idea. In a great many cases, as I indicated before six o'clock, a great part of this money is not going to be forthcoming because this very bill has made provisions for the government to have the first claim on these cash advances.
As I also pointed out, about two-thirds of our farmers in western Canada will receive only the small amount of approximately $900 and if you take off the amount of money which would be owing under the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act there is not going to be very much left. I would recommend to the government and to every member of this house that clause 18 be withdrawn because the government is certainly setting an example by including this clause and encouraging all other creditors to make pressing demands on the farmer in order to get as much of this cash advance as they can before the farmer has an opportunity to use it for the needs of his family and to pay up all the small obligations incurred throughout the community.
Now at best this legislation is of a very temporary nature. It cannot be considered in any sense as a solution of the farmers' problems. It is certainly time that the government brought down measures or at least indicated to this house their intention of making good their election promises, not only to regain our lost markets but to get some new ones. Now nothing very noticeable has been done so far in the way of fulfilling these promises. They turned down the only practicable offer and that was the one proposed by the United Kingdom government. We had been given to understand from the speech from the throne and throughout this debate that this government was going to bring down legislation which would increase our sales but when I read over the speech which the Minister of Agriculture made on October 28 I was somewhat confused, for on page 458, towards the latter part of the first column the minister had this to say about the prospects of increased sales of our agricultural products.
Our sales to the United Kingdom and Europe this crop year should compare favourably with last crop year.
Now that certainly does not indicate any bright prospects for agriculture; it means in fact that this government does not intend to do anything different in the way of increasing our sales from what was done by the former government. In fact up to the present moment our sales have been less than for the corresponding period last year.

The minister himself does not indicate that it will be any better than it was last year. Now unless something is done to increase our sales abroad it is certainly not going to bring much relief to the agricultural industry in western Canada. The Minister of Agriculture when presenting this bill the other day on behalf of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) made reference to his trip to the United States and the discussions there with respect to the prospects of increased trade. He said hopes were quite good and that things were going along quite satisfactorily as far as discussions with the United States were concerned. He condemned the United States government for the methods they employed in getting rid of their surplus products and referred particularly to the give-away program and the barter deals. He said the impression was, as has also been indicated in the press, that these transactions would cease or at least be lessened. However when you read the minister's speech I do not think you can get that out of it at all because at page 458 of Hansard of October 28, the Minister of Agriculture had this to say:
"I should perhaps explain to the house that, in effect, this barter program has been only a concealed form of additional subsidy by the United States. The result has been to reduce normal United States commercial sales as well as hurt the Canadian competitive position."
Here is the most important part:
"We found that our United States colleagues agreed in the main with this point of view and they affirmed to us their intention that before approving further barter transactions they would require proof that those transactions would result in additional sales."
It surely cannot be true to say that this is any change in the United States policy or that any promises given to our government would have the effect of lessening the barter deals. This cabinet committee commission which was sent by the government to the United States came back and reported that prospects were better. What could be further from the truth? The United States told that committee and the minister has in his own words told the house that those transactions will result in additional sales. For whom? For the United States, certainly not for us.
Of course the United States in their disposal program has never adopted any other attitude and these give-away programs and barter deals have one purpose and one purpose only, to increase the sales of the United States surplus products. That is exactly what they told the Canadian delegation in Washington and anybody who thinks this government is making proposals which are going to increase our foreign markets had better take a closer look at the words of the Minister of Agriculture the other day.

Mr. Speaker, I want to rise at this time to let people know where I stand with regard to this bill. I want to support it, of course, as hon. members know, although I do not think it

Grain
goes quite far enough. It seems there is nothing we can do about that. Someone said today that half a loaf is better than none, and I am looking on the measure now before us in that way.
I have risen in this house on many occasions to plead the cause of the farmer and never got anything. This time I am getting a little, and I am quite well pleased. When farmers get into difficulties they go into the towns, and when that happens they compete for employment on the labour market. Surely it is right that the government should try to keep the farmers on the land. As I stated, many of those who leave the farm go into the towns, see the bright lights, find that they can make a living there, and then decide they are not going back again. That is one of the reasons why we have fewer farmers today.
This bill will be of some help to agriculture, though I think everyone agrees it is not enough. But it is something. The position of the Canadian farmer today when he cannot sell his crop is a serious one. Hon. members must realize that he has no wages, no other source of revenue of any kind. When he gets his advance payment he will have to share it with the storekeeper, the oil man, the implement agent and, no doubt, the bank, because on the farmers' dollar, or business-call it what you like-the whole agricultural economy depends. The advance payment will be like a blood transfusion to a sick man, but it is going to take a lot of transfusions to bring the agricultural economy back into a healthy state again.
It has been suggested that the grain farmer should raise hogs and cattle. We have a surplus of wheat at the present time, and I am sure some of the hon. members who were here in 1943 and 1944 when we were producing hogs in a bigger way than any other country in the world know how many hogs we are capable of producing and realize that we would have a surplus of hogs and, no doubt, a surplus of cattle in three years' time if this policy was followed.
I think that by now almost everything has been said that could be said both for and against the bill, and I suggest that we should have a vote in order to enable the farmers to get the advance payment. However, there is one point I wish to draw to the minister's attention. In some districts, where we have five or six elevators in line, a farmer has the privilege of delivering to any one of them. But if we move further out into the country we arrive at points which have only one elevator. A man living in that area can go nowhere else; he is bound to sell to that one
elevator, and take all the dirt that the elevator agent likes to dish up to him. Why cannot the government give him the right to go to one other elevator, the one either to the east or west?
Since I was appealing to my colleagues to let us have this vote and let the farmer get the money, I think it would be better if I raised this matter again later when the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) come up for consideration, and explain further what I have in mind. I think the minister knows already, because this is obviously something that should be corrected.

My reason for supporting this legislation differs from the reason of the western grain growers. Mr. Speaker, I fully intended to let this measure go through without saying anything about it; but representatives from the grain-growing areas and a good many others have taken part in the debate and perhaps my constituents would be disappointed if I did not

have at least a few words to say on it and I can assure you they will not be long.
I have heard a good many optimistic speeches during last night and today about what this bill will do toward putting money in the hands of the farmers. When I listened to some of the new members sitting on the government benches I had the impression that they seemed to think that the government of the day has all the answers. I want to warn them at this point that this is a huge problem and it is going to take all the brains that they have and probably a few more before it is solved.
As far as putting money into the hands of the farmers is concerned-that is what I am mainly interested in-there is one clause in this bill that I am a little worried about. This clause says that if a farmer has borrowed money under the interim financing act of 1956 that money will have to be repaid out of those cash advances. In my district last year our quota was four bushels to the acre and a good many of the farmers in the district were not able to deliver even that amount of grain. When I left home this year very few of them had been able to deliver the initial quota although they were on a one-bushel quota. The people who were not able to deliver more than five bushels per acre last year y/ere not in a position to repay those loans; it was impossible for them to do so. If, when they get an advance this year on this year's crop, they have to repay those loans there will not be very much money in their pockets.
That is the question that is bothering me. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) who is piloting the bill through the house may have the answer to it. However, I just want to warn the government that many of the farmers will not get much benefit from this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, because of the number of speeches that have been made on this bill it may be interpreted that hon. members coming from ridings that are not predominantly wheatgrowing ones are not entirely sympathetic to the bill. It may also be miscontrued that hon. members on this side of the house are also hopeful that when this legislation is passed something further is going to be done to assist the diversified farmer or the small tree fruit grower.
In my riding we have tree fruit growers in certain areas who are in quite dire circumstances. These people market their product through a central selling agency, receiving perhaps a small down payment. Yet they have capital tied up for a year or maybe two years.

It is conceivable that they may wish to borrow money on the certificates which they have. There are other circumstances which are even more trying in that many of the small fruit growers, even this year, were obliged to allow the fruit either to rot on the trees or to pick it and take it to a suitable dump because they were unable to market their fruit. Only 80 miles away from where my home is cherries were selling at a price of $8 a crate. Yet they were rotting on the trees because there was no market. All of these difficulties will have to be ironed out.
I am going to support the bill. Since I have been in this house for the past nine years there have been more bills and more measures dealing with the wheat problem and the wheat farmers on the prairies and I have supported them all along the line. I realize that they are under grave difficulties at this time. But I do not want some of the new members on the government side or the members of the C.C.F. party to think that I swallow everything that they say about the conditions or about why these conditions have arisen. For instance, the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) had this to say last evening about the reasons for the circumstances that prevail on the prairies at this time. I am reading from page 491 of Hansard:
The producers are not responsible for the condition which exists but they are forced under legislation to sell their grain to the wheat board.
Of course he qualified that statement by saying this:
They asked for it and the government adopted the plan.
He might as well say, "They asked for it and they got it." The farmers asked for the wheat board; they wanted it set up. It was not the miners in Kimberley or the fruit growers in Creston. The farmers asked for it, it was set up. Now, of course, they say that it was because the board was operating under a Liberal government that they did not sell grain. If a board is set up and is going to be directed entirely by any government, then it is not a board at all. I therefore do not think the blame is entirely on the administration. Of course, the hon. member for Yorkton started to say that it was the administration that was responsible for the situation and then he went on to say that it was the give-away policies of the United States. At least we have in this western hemisphere some countries that are prepared to do something for the underdeveloped countries. They are willing to give some wheat away. That should be the charitable attitude of many of the members of this house and they should not say that the circumstances under which they
Grain
find themselves are brought about owing to the charity of some other government.
There was another member over here who dragged out that old story that we have heard for nine years. I hope that all the new members over there do not feel obligated to tell us about the circumstances in which they contributed $600 million to the economy of this country by having a fixed price during the war and immediately after it. We have heard all that before and, in my opinion, much of it is nonsense. We had price fixing during the war. We had wage regulations during the war. If they want the truth of the matter, I can recall working in the mines producing the lead and zinc for the war effort, and I can recall the time when up to 300 or 400 miners sold their automobiles out on the prairies where wheat was being sold. The miners just could not get the gasoline. They were being taxed to such an extent that they could not afford to operate their cars. The cars were being sold out on the prairies. I am not kicking about this matter. However, let us not have too much of this talk about hard luck. We are going along with it but some time we are just going to get tired.
There is another speech to which I take some exception. I think it is despicable that a member of this house, having sat with one of his hon. colleagues for many years, should stoop to attack that member as if that member were completely dishonest, and charge him with certain things when it was impossible for him to appear on the floor of the house and defend himself. I am referring to the speech made last evening by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson). The hon. member seemed to imply that the former member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre was running a dishonest bootleg joint, not in rye but in wheat. He had this to say. It is an offer to buy wheat provided that the farmer delivers it to a point specified in this advertisement for a cent a pound. This applies to No. 5 and No. 6 wheat which today are selling on the market for 97 cents a bushel.

But he fails to point out that the freight charges on a bushel of wheat to the lakehead is 20 cents a bushel. Therefore, if his figures are correct,-and of

course I have no reason to doubt them- that would make the price of that wheat delivered to the elevator 97 cents less 20 cents which is 77 cents.
