I think you are speaking about your own statement when you make that interjection.
There is one part of this bill that I feel is far from adequate. 1 had hoped that when the government was considering the payment of cash advances that in setting forth the quota on which cash advances would be made they would have guaranteed that the farmer would have an opportunity of delivering grain against that quota so that at the end of that crop year, or at some later date if the quota should not be available, the farmer would have an opportunity of delivering, in this case six bushels of wheat, against an advance that was being made in the current crop year. X had hoped that the government would not do as they have done in this legislation, and that is give no guarantee at all as to the quota that the farmer may have at any given marketing point.
Moreover, there is a stipulation in precise terms that if the 6-bushel quota is not available at any marketing point and an individual farmer has taken advantage of this legislation, the balance he owes will be a first claim against grain he draws in the succeeding crop year. In other words, there is no guarantee in this legislation as to marketing opportunities that western wheat producers will have in this crop year or in any other crop year.
This legislation is going to be of advantage on a very temporary basis. It is going to do exactly what the minister has said. It is going to mean that out of the national treasury this crop year will come somewhere between $2 million and $3 million to pay the interest charged against the money advanced under this legislation, and that is the sum total of the real effect in economic terms. It will do the other things we have been saying it will do, should do, and which are of advantage, namely it will make a large sum of money available within a matter of weeks.
The benefit during this crop year is going to be small, particularly small because there is no guarantee that the 6-bushel quota will be available or that the farmer will have an opportunity to deliver six bushels. How could that be done? It could be done very simply. It may not be possible, it is true, to have a 6-bushel quota at every marketing point, although as other members have said the promises that were held out to the western electorate caused us to expect that a 6-bushel quota would be no trouble at all. If a 6-bushel quota is not available at a marketing point, a farmer has not an opportunity of discharging his obligation under this legislation. It would not be difficult to provide

a supplementary quota at that marketing point equal to the amount of the quota that could not be delivered in the current crop year. In other words, if farmers at a marketing point had an opportunity of delivering five bushels on the quota this year, then a supplementary quota of one bushel could be made available in the following crop year. In this way all producers in the various marketing points would have the same opportunity of delivering grain.
Under this legislation, however, there is no guarantee as to what market will be available for grain. I feel that is a very serious omission. If we had turned the corner, if we had reached the bottom and were on the way up in regard to markets, we would not be as concerned as we are. From August 1 to date under the present administration there has been a very substantial drop in exports of Canadian grain as compared with a similar period the year before. There has been a very substantial drop in markets. In introducing this legislation the minister said it was expected the measure might cost the federal treasury something in the neighbourhood of $2.25 million, and that is true. This $2.25 million will accrue to the benefit of the producer. During the current crop year 1956 from August 1 to October 16-I am quoting now from the board of grain commissioners for Canada, statistics branch, Canadian grain position, Wednesday, October 16, 1957-farmers marketed a total of 118.9 million bushels of grain, this year, in the same period marketings had dropped to 93.3 million bushels.
In other words, from August 1 to October 16 of this year farm marketings of all grain were down 22 per cent as compared with last year. If I were to make a very conservative estimate I might say that farmers, because of the drop in marketings, have lost in revenue over $30 million.
So from August 1 of this year as compared with the same period last year, there is a drop in farm marketings to the farmers from the sale of grain of over $30 million.
With regard to exports, in the same period this year they are down as compared with last year. I am quoting now from the export figures for all grain. A year ago the total was 78.8 million bushels; for the same period this year the total was 60.6 million bushels, or a drop of 23 per cent.
Farmers by the thousands in the three western provinces are facing imminent bankruptcy. It is in my opinion only a matter of one or two years or perhaps even a few months-unless something is done to correct the basic situation, which is a falling off in markets and in agricultural prices together
Grain
with an increase in the cost of production- before thousands of farmers will be driven off their land.
The legislation now before this house will help for a few months but it will not help materially for a longer period unless something is done to correct the situation in regard to our loss of markets and to improve our sales to the export markets of the world.
I do not know what the government will be able to accomplish in this field. We in this group have advanced policies from time to time which we believe will restore and increase our markets for agricultural products-the acceptance of sterling, sales on the basis of long-term contracts, the setting up of an export-import board and so on. We have a policy directed to increasing our sales and exports of agricultural products. One would have expected when the minister was introducing the bill to the house and there was a short review of our export prospects that there would have been some statement from the official opposition as to their present position and their policy. However, there has been no such statement and the official opposition has not advanced a single suggestion to restore our markets or to gain new markets. As a matter of fact in this house a few days ago one very prominent and outstanding member of the official opposition made a careful speech in which he gave the government a dressing down for not having done something in this field, for not having advanced a policy and for not having achieved great things. Then, when he was asked what was the policy of the official opposition, here are his words:

objective is a good one. It has been to reduce Canada's purchases from the United States by some 15 per cent and to transfer those purchases to European and soft currency countries, in other words to countries which might purchase greater quantities of goods from us.

The long-range view with regard to our wheat entails a forward-looking policy with regard to general production, and it may well be that progressively over the years our acreage devoted solely to the growing of wheat should be appreciably reduced and greater emphasis should be placed on diversified crops and on the livestock industry.
Then, in a later interchange he was talking about 20 million acres of wheat. Of course the acreage is down to just about 20 million acres this year but if the government is suggesting, through the Minister of Trade and Commerce that wheat production should be reduced and that livestock production should be increased he is talking about something which affects the Minister of Agriculture. I now ask the Minister of Agriculture to say what agricultural products he would like to see reduced and what livestock products he wants to see increased. Does he want to see an increase in the production of beef; does he want to see an increase in the production of pork.
I have looked over the markets since the Minister of Trade and Commerce made this statement and from a quick review since that time I would say there has been a drop of anywhere from $1 to $1.50 a hundredweight for good steers; since he made this statement the price of hogs has dropped by something like $7, from $32 to $25 within a few weeks. Does the Minister of Agriculture agree with the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that wheat acreage should be reduced and livestock production increased.
As I see the situation, and from what I have heard from members from all parts of the country who have been taking part in this debate, the agricultural market and prices in other parts of Canada are in just as bad a mess as they are on the prairies. Is it going to help livestock markets and prices in eastern Canada for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to suggest that western farmers should reduce their wheat acreage and increase the production of livestock. Is the farmer going to take land out of wheat production. If so he will likely do what he has done in the past, namely increase the production of barley and oats. Well, there is a glut

of oats and there is a glut of barley; there is a surplus of pork if you can judge by the market prices.
This government has not found an answer to the critical problem which faces agricultural producers across Canada, the increasing prices which have to be paid for agricultural products in relation to the farmer's income. I think the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce which I have read to the house was ill considered. It was a statement which was opposed by farm organizations right across the country, and if this is the best the Minister of Trade and Commerce can do as a suggestion for improving agricultural conditions in Canada it demonstates to me that worsening conditions as a result of falling markets are likely to continue.
Many members have made reference to western Canada in this debate and spoken of what they would like to have in other parts of this country. To all those hon. members who are saying that this measure is just for the prairies, or that it seems to represent special treatment for people on the prairies, I would say this: many years ago the grain producers in the prairie provinces came to the conclusion that they would do better if they marketed their grain through a central agency, in this case established under federal legislation, than they would if they relied upon the open market, or private trade, or free enterprise. I suggest to those from other parts of Canada who want and need improved prices for their products, or who need better legislation for their constituents, that they should first of all propose that the government in co-operation with the producers be prepared to establish marketing boards in line with the producers' wishes and that then, after having established marketing boards in which the federal government takes a direct interest if so requested by the producers, they should ask for initial prices at reasonable limits, cash advances, and all the other things that are a necessary part of an orderly system of marketing.

At this time we began to consolidate small farms into larger ones and brought into use big strings of equipment and as a consequence there was a greater production of wheat. We should have been keeping pace with that increase in production by making available increased storage facilities.
As I have said on other occasions, providing increased storage facilities for grains or other farm products that could benefit the whole country is, in my opinion, the responsibility of the government of the country. I have constantly said that individuals in this nation should not be expected to do for themselves that which is prohibitively expensive or which they cannot do nearly so well as the government could and it is the role of government to accept responsibility in this regard.

speechtext: The hon. member for Assini-boia stated that the sum total of the economic effect of this legislation is only $2 million to $3 million in interest which will be put out or help that will be given in that way to farmers. When he made that statement he must surely have completely lost sight of the fact that I pointed out when I started this speech the great general benefit to the farmers and to the western economy of this $100 million to $150 million of cash which is going to go into their hands.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I might say to the minister that I was talking about the full crop year and not an immediate period.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Very well. The hon. member for Assiniboia also said that there was no guarantee that the 6-bushel quota will be capable of being filled. Certainly there is no guarantee in this legislation. This legislation does not pretend to guarantee that result. But I can tell the hon. member this. We believe there is every expectation that this 6-bushel quota will be filled. The scheme is based on the expectation that it will be filled. That is why the 6-bushel quota is mentioned in the scheme. We have every confidence and every expectation that the 6-bushel quota will be filled. Nobody can guarantee that it will be

filled. As somebody here said this afternoon, nobody can guarantee that it will be filled. Nobody can look into the future. However, there is very good expectation that it will be filled.
The hon. member also said that there had been a substantial drop in exports since August. This is just not so. I have here the list showing the exports right back to 1927. The substantial and big drop in exports took place back in the months of January, February, March, April, May and June and the situation has been improving since that time. As a matter of fact, back in April of this year approximately 15 million bushels were sold and in the previous April-that is 1956- 33 million bushels were sold, well over twice as much, and nearly the same situation prevailed in May and so on, but when we get up to August we find that 29.7 million bushels were exported in 1956 and 27.1 million bushels this year.
In September there were 27.4 million bushels in 1956, and in this year-the estimated figure is not quite complete yet- there is between 24 million and 24.5 million bushels. In other words, the figures for the period August-September are quite close to last year's figures. The big drop was in the period back in the winter, spring, and early summer.

No, I want to finish this right now. The hon. member for Assiniboia also asked what agricultural products did I wish to see increased, and do I agree that wheat acreage should be reduced? Yes, Mr. Speaker, I do agree that there should be some reduction in wheat acreage. During the last four years in this house, as the hon. member probably recalls, I have been saying we should take a long-range view in regard to the general agricultural situation, and particularly the wheat situation. I have said that it was foolish for us to continue planning for the same amount of wheat every year and constantly building up a surplus; that we should divert some of our land into other types of crops. As to the types of crops in which I think we could increase production, I would mention beef and sheep as two of them. I would be quite glad to go into this subject in more detail at a later date.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) said that we should call on the Right Hon. C. D. Howe to help us out at the present time by building some elevators. I doubt whether it would be wise for us to call on the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, no matter

how good an elevator builder he may be, because during all the years he handled the wheat business he certainly made a mess of it.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE RIVER JOINT BOARD OF ENGINEERS
speechtext:
1.	Who are the members of the St. Lawrence river joint board of engineers?
2.	What are the duties of the board?
3.	Has the board approved of the plans of the respective governments of Canada and the United States for the transfer of 14-foot navigation from the Canadian side to the American side?
4.	Is the board satisfied that this plan will be effective and in operation by July 1, 1958? What effect will this plan have upon traffic over the south channel low level bridge at Cornwall?
5.	Will traffic be interrupted over this bridge after April 1, 1958? If so, what alternative means of transportation is being provided to residents of Canada and the United States in this area?
6.	Has the board approved of the plans of the respective power entities for channel enlargements from Chimney point to the control dam at Iroquois?
7.	What do these plans contemplate so far as the requirements of navigation are concerned?
8.	Are they on schedule?
9.	Will they meet the requirements of navigation in all respects when (a) transfer of 14-foot navigation from Canada to United States on July 1, 1958, takes place; (b) 27-foot navigation opens in April, 1959?
Answer by: Mr. MacDonald, Parliamentary
Assistant, for the Minister of Transport:
The St. Lawrence river joint board of engineers advise as follows:
1.	Members for Canada: Hon. George Hees and Mr. Chas. Gavsie; alternates: Mr. H. W. Lea and Mr. Geo. H. Kohl. Members for United States: Hon. Wilber M. Brucker and Hon. Jerome Kuykendall; alternates: Maj. Gen. Chas. G. Holle and Mr. Francis L. Adams.
2.	(a) To review, co-ordinate and approve, in behalf of the governments of Canada and United States, the plans and specifications of the works for the development of power in the international rapids section, submitted by the joint builders, namely the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario and the power authority of the state of New York; (b) to insure that the works are constructed in accordance therewith as approved.
3.	The board has reviewed the most recent plans of both power and seaway entities for works to be constructed to permit the transfer of 14-foot navigation from the Canadian side to the American side and on the basis of these plans and the accompanying schedules, the board considers that the plans are satisfactory.
4.	Yes, if the above schedules are met. As to the effect on traffic, the plans require

5.	Yes. Traffic will be diverted to a ferry.
6.	Yes.
7.	A minimum channel width of 600 feet, a minimum depth of 29.5 feet based on method of regulation 12-A-9 and a maximum velocity of 4 foot per second.
8.	No, see answer to question No. 9.
9.	(a) Yes; (b) yes, although in some limited reaches the permanent channels may not be completed to full width by April, 1959.

subtopic: CANADIAN COAST GUARD
CANADIAN COAST GUARD
speechtext:
What steps, if any, since assuming office has the government taken toward the establishment of a Canadian coast guard?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister
of Transport):
The functions that are normally considered to be the duty of a coast guard are performed in Canada by several agencies of government, in particular my department, the Department of National Defence and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. All these agencies continue to give attention to improvement of their ability to carry out their responsibilities but no decision has been taken to remove functions from these departments and place them under a new and separate agency.
